goal: Explain this OpenMP scheduling paper to undergraduates and an unfamiliar professor, with minimal slides and patient notes.

approval.evidence: User replied go ahead to approval of the outline and skipping further confirmation steps.

deck_context.source_summary: We compare 12-candidate scheduling search with a training-guided four-candidate shortlist on one four-core WSL2 machine. Guided 4 saves 65.0% tuning wall time and 65.9% tuning CPU time. At 50 useful loops after EXTRA calibration and with a CACHED model, total elapsed saving is about 27.5%. No clear benefit when exploratory executions already perform useful work.
deck_context.core_claim: Count both choosing cost and useful execution cost, including a share of training. Benefits are conditional; model ranking is not proven necessary.
canonical_terms: scheduler = rule distributing loop iterations to threads
Full 12 is a finite noisy search, not a true optimum

slides.title: When is the trade-off worth it?
slides.intent: One simple understandable claim; retain the approved research facts.
key_points: The tests must be additional work that can genuinely be avoided.
The model must already exist or be reused enough to repay its cost.
The chosen scheduler's execution quality must be acceptable.

local_context.approved_content_and_visual_instructions:
Visible bullets:
- The tests must be additional work that can genuinely be avoided.
- The model must already exist or be reused enough to repay its cost.
- The chosen scheduler's execution quality must be acceptable.

Centered equation: time saved choosing > extra execution time + share of preparation cost.
Reminder box: “One machine, three workload families; no guarantee for every new program.”
Role: analysis and decision rule. This is the paper's worthwhile-exchange inequality with the prior charge included. Notes explain the noisy reference, 12 independent input clusters, and large occasional quality penalties.
